raw.answer: A Taiwanese father and an Italian mother, who were never married, fought over their young daughter. A Taiwan court ordered the father to hand her over to the mother so she could live in Italy for now, and the Supreme Court let that stand. The Constitutional Court found that the Supreme Court's ruling violated the Constitution, struck it down and sent the case back.
raw.held: The Supreme Court's 2022 ruling (111年度台簡抗字第13號) is unconstitutional, is set aside and is sent back to the Supreme Court. The challenge to the other rulings (the father's second, separate request) was not accepted.

points.text: The Court accepted the challenge to the Supreme Court ruling because it was a final ruling after all appeals. It also raised important constitutional questions about children's best interests and about the child being heard.
The challenge to the other rulings, which rejected the father's own request for an interim order, was not accepted. That rejection did not change anyone's current rights or duties.

A child's best interests are central to the constitutional protection of the child's personality rights and dignity. Even in interim orders, courts must weigh all favorable and unfavorable factors and investigate as far as circumstances allow.

Courts must respect the child's wishes and let the child speak, and must seriously consider what the child says. Continuity of the child's living environment is also an important principle, so a child should not be moved to another country temporarily without very urgent and strong need.

The lower courts never considered the girl's wishes. They also did not consider whether Taiwan, where she had lived about 2 years 9 months and was doing well, had become her new habitual home. They did not examine whether moving her to Italy was truly necessary, and the Supreme Court upheld this.

Before an interim order handing over a child, and also on appeal, the child should be given a chance to speak. A court-appointed child representative or records of earlier statements elsewhere cannot replace this, so the failure breached due process.

who: The unmarried parents in the case

raw.answer: A man held in pre-trial detention during an investigation had his detention extended by a court, and his defense lawyer appealed on his behalf. The appeal was rejected, and he asked the Constitutional Court whether the Code of Criminal Procedure gives defense lawyers the right to appeal such rulings. The court decided that, read together, the rules let a defense lawyer appeal detention or extended-detention rulings for the defendant's benefit, unless the defendant clearly says otherwise.
raw.held: Read together, Articles 403 and 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure mean a defense lawyer may appeal a court's detention or extended-detention ruling for the defendant's benefit, unless the defendant has expressly said the opposite. This is required for the rules to be consistent with the Constitution's protection of personal liberty (Art. 8) and the right to bring legal action (Art. 16).

points.text: Defendants have a constitutional right to an effective defense, including help from a lawyer, and the right to appeal a ruling is an important part of that defense. A lawyer's ability to appeal for the defendant is therefore protected, unless the defendant expressly objects.

Detention is the most intrusive compulsory measure against personal liberty. A detained defendant is cut off from the outside world, finds it hard to research the law and write an appeal, and has only 5 days to appeal, so needs a lawyer's timely help.
The Code allows lawyers to appeal judgments for the defendant (Art. 346), but the appeals part has no similar provision. This created doubt about whether a lawyer could appeal a ruling.

Article 419 applies the rules on appeals of judgments to appeals of rulings, because the two serve similar purposes. This does not apply where the appeals part has its own exclusive special rule, such as those on appealable matters, the 5-day period, and the 10-day deadline for the appeal court.

Article 403 only distinguishes parties from non-parties such as witnesses and experts, and sets no exclusive rule barring defense lawyers. So defense lawyers can use Article 346 through Article 419 to appeal for the defendant.

who: Legislators and agencies reviewing the Code

raw.answer: A National Taiwan University law professor failed a re-evaluation of his teaching, research and service, and argued that the college's evaluation rules (Articles 5 to 8 of its implementing rules) were unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court held that the rules are clear enough, follow fair procedure, and are a proportionate limit on teachers' freedom to pursue their occupation.
raw.held: The court held that Articles 5 to 8 of the NTU College of Law teacher evaluation implementing rules do not violate the clarity principle or due process. Their limit on teachers' occupational freedom also meets the proportionality principle in Article 23 and does not violate the right to work in Article 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: Teacher evaluation can lead to non-renewal or dismissal, so it limits occupational freedom and affects the right to work. Because it is a limit on a subjective condition and universities have academic autonomy, the court reviewed it under a lenient standard.

The rules are clear: they list the items evaluated, set minimum thresholds, and require an average of 70 points. Their meaning is understandable, especially to law faculty, who are the people they apply to.
Teachers can foresee what to prepare and the consequences of failing. Faculty help make the rules, and the rules can be reviewed by courts through administrative remedies.

The scoring method and procedure are objective, credible and fair enough, and reflect the college's own character, so university autonomy should be respected. Evaluators' academic judgment gets considerable deference, but courts can still review scoring that is unlawful, clearly improper, based on wrong facts, or arbitrary.

The process protects the teacher's rights to be heard, to be informed and to seek remedies: the teacher is notified to explain, given reasons and improvement advice, given a two-year improvement period, and told of appeal routes before any non-renewal or dismissal.

The evaluation system has a legitimate purpose, which is raising teaching and research quality and protecting students' right to education. Evaluation with a re-evaluation after an improvement period reasonably helps achieve that purpose, so it meets the proportionality principle.

raw.answer: A trial court asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether a traffic law is unconstitutional. The law let police forcibly send drivers who caused a crash and refused or could not take a breath alcohol test to have their blood drawn and tested. The court held the rule unconstitutional because it lacked judicial oversight and privacy protections and was too broad, and it gave two years for a fix with interim safeguards.
raw.held: Article 35, paragraph 5 of the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (2013 version) loses effect within two years of the judgment. Meanwhile, police must get a prosecutor's permit before forced blood testing, or report within 24 hours in urgent cases. The challenge to the lower-level rules was not accepted.

points.text: Forced blood testing seriously limits personal liberty, bodily integrity and information privacy, so the court reviewed it strictly.
Preventing drunk driving is a especially important public interest, and forced blood testing can serve it where there is a reasonable need and reason to think drink-driving caused the crash.
The rule goes too far when a crash may have had other causes, so forcing blood tests every time is not the least harmful means.
Allowing 'other specimens' to be taken is unconstitutional because drunk driving is judged only by breath or blood alcohol levels, so this does not help the goal.
The rule lacked due process: no prior review by a judge or prosecutor, no later reporting, no remedy, and it let non-police traffic inspectors act.
Lawmakers did not set by law what is tested, how results may be used, or how specimens are kept and destroyed, which breaches the legal-reservation principle on privacy.

who: Drivers who cause crashes and refuse or cannot take a breath test

raw.answer: Several people whose criminal-proceeds were ordered confiscated, and two judges, challenged a Criminal Code rule (Article 2, paragraph 2) saying confiscation follows the law in force at the time of the court's ruling. They argued it applied the new confiscation rules backward to conduct that was already finished. The Constitutional Court held that, as far as it covers confiscating criminal proceeds under Article 38-1 paragraphs 1 and 2, the rule is constitutional.
raw.held: The rule that confiscation applies the law at the time of the judgment is not unconstitutional as it concerns confiscation of criminal proceeds under Article 38-1(1) and (2). The petitions of persons one to five (and the judicial petitions of persons six and seven) were rejected or not accepted accordingly, and some other parts were not accepted.

points.text: Confiscating criminal proceeds is not a criminal penalty: it does not require blame or a conviction, it can reach bad-faith third parties, the amount is tied to the proceeds and not to the seriousness of the crime, and it cannot be replaced by labor service. So the principle of no punishment without law does not apply.
The legislature's purpose was to restore a lawful property order and remove the incentive to commit crime, not to take away people's pre-existing property or to punish.

Counting proceeds on a relative gross basis (without deducting costs tainted by illegality) does not make confiscation a penalty. It follows the risk allocation of unjust-enrichment law and only restores the earlier position.
The rule is not truly retroactive: the unlawful property situation created by the proceeds continues until they are taken, so applying the new rule to it does not breach the ban on retroactivity.

Offenders and bad-faith third parties have no protectable trust in keeping criminal proceeds, since the property was tainted from the start. The old law's gaps, and the important public interest in fixing them, support the reform.

who: People ordered to have criminal proceeds confiscated
Bad-faith third parties who received criminal proceeds

raw.answer: A Taipei court hearing a civil-service personnel case asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether rules letting agencies dismiss public servants through a year-end 'Grade D' performance rating are constitutional. The court held that these rules do not conflict with Article 77 of the Constitution or with the right to hold public office under Article 18. It declined to hear the challenge to a separate administrative procedure provision.
raw.held: The provisions in the Civil Service Performance Evaluation Act (Articles 6(3)(4), 7(1)(4) and the latter part of Article 8) that allow dismissal on a Grade D rating are not unconstitutional under Articles 77 and 18. The remaining parts of the petition were not accepted.

points.text: Dismissal is part of the executive's core personnel power, and a court cannot fully replace the agency in making the first decision, so agency dismissal fits the separation of powers.
Article 77 does not contain a 'unified discipline' principle; it was meant to stop the Control Yuan from both impeaching and judging, and it does not cover administrative sanctions.
Discipline and administrative sanctions differ in purpose and effect and have long run side by side; Grade D dismissal only ends the current post and does not bar future public service.
The constitutional amendment changing 'appointment' to 'appointment and dismissal' confirms dismissal belongs to the executive branch and does not hand it to courts.

Earlier interpretations accepted the dual track, and after Interpretation No. 785 public servants can seek court relief against dismissals, so such dismissals need not be treated as judicial discipline.

Dismissal serves the important public interest of removing unfit staff and is substantially related to that aim, so it does not violate the right to hold public office; the court also urged authorities to clarify how the two tracks relate.

who: Public servants rated Grade D and dismissed
Government agencies that employ public servants

raw.answer: 38 legislators challenged Taiwan's 2020 Farmland Irrigation Act, which turned the irrigation associations into part of the government and moved their assets to the state. The Constitutional Court found the challenged provisions constitutional on every point and rejected the request for a temporary order. It treated the move from public-law corporation to government agency as a policy choice, not a constitutional violation.
raw.held: The challenged articles (1, 18(1) and (3), 19(3), 23(1) and (5), and 34(2)) are not unconstitutional: they are not unclear, do not violate freedom of association or property rights, and do not breach non-retroactivity or reliance protection. The request for a temporary order was dismissed.

points.text: 'Reform' in Articles 1 and 23 is clear enough, because the earlier amendment to the associations' general act and the new Act's other provisions show it means turning the associations into government bodies. Once the general act stopped applying, their public-law corporation status ended.

Freedom of association covers private groups, not creating public-law corporations. The associations were set up by law, so ending their corporate status does not infringe members' freedom of association.

A public-law corporation's property is public property, not constitutionally protected property. Assets of the Japanese-era water unions and of the later associations were acquired through their public-law status, and members had no property rights in them, so the state taking them over does not violate property rights.
Public-law corporations exist to carry out state tasks, and the state may adjust or dissolve them. They cannot invoke non-retroactivity or reliance protection against that.

The rules on irrigation management bodies and personnel do not conflict with the constitutional amendment on organizational law, because the Farmland Irrigation Act can set them out itself. The Irrigation Agency is a transitional body with a basis in organizational rules, and irrigation authority has rested with the central government.
Since the case was decided, no temporary order was needed. Whether to use a public-law corporation or government agency model is a policy choice, not a question of constitutionality.

raw.answer: Five city and county councils passed local food-safety rules that banned any detectable ractopamine (a feed additive, 'lai-ji') in imported meat, and the central government declared the rules void or refused to approve them. The Constitutional Court held that setting safe residue limits for imported meat is a matter for central legislation, so the central government's actions were constitutional. It declined to hear the remaining requests.
raw.held: The court held that safe-residue standards for beta-agonists in imported meat and meat products are for the central government to legislate. It also held that the Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Executive Yuan did not exceed their constitutional power to supervise local government when they voided or refused to approve the local rules, and it dismissed the remaining requests.

points.text: The constitution sets up a unitary state, not a federal one. Local self-government lawmaking remains bound by the constitution and central law, and local rules that conflict with central law are invalid.

Local lawmaking is limited to people and things inside the locality's own area. A local rule that has a direct and close real effect outside the area is a cross-regional or national matter and cannot be left to each locality.

Residue standards for meat sold nationwide must be uniform, because different local limits would directly affect buyers, sellers and transport outside each area. Under the constitution's provisions on commerce and public health this is central legislative business, and the Food Safety Act authorizes only the central authority to set the standard.

The five local ordinances, though worded as applying to local residents, affect people and things outside their areas. They therefore went beyond local lawmaking power and conflicted with the Food Safety Act and the constitution.

The earlier Interpretation No. 738 does not help the petitioners. There, central law gave local authorities power and the rules affected only locals; here the local standards lack authorization, contradict central rules, and affect people outside the area.

The zero-detection rules also conflict with the constitution's guarantee of free circulation of goods within the country. Lawfully imported ractopamine meat was effectively made illegal locally, even meat merely passing through, which obstructs the domestic market.

Because the local standards lacked authorization and conflicted with central law, the supervising authorities could declare the ordinances void or refuse approval. Whether the central standard protects health well enough is a risk-assessment question outside this case.

who: Local councils and governments of cities and counties

raw.answer: A defense lawyer attended a prosecutor's questioning of a defendant. The prosecutor seized the lawyer's notes and barred further note-taking, and the court rejected the lawyer's challenge because the law lists no such ground for appeal. Taiwan's Constitutional Court held that the lack of any way to ask a court to review such restrictions violates the constitutional right to court access, and it set an interim procedure until the law is amended.
raw.held: The law is unconstitutional to the extent it gives no way to challenge a prosecutor's order limiting or barring a lawyer's presence, note-taking or statements at questioning. The authorities have 2 years to amend the law, and until then the existing procedure in Article 416 may be used to ask the court to cancel such orders. The remaining part of the petition was not accepted.

points.text: The Constitution protects a suspect's or defendant's right to effective help from a defense lawyer, starting at the investigation stage.

That right includes the lawyer being present, taking notes and giving opinions during questioning, and the lawyer may seek relief in the lawyer's own name for the client's benefit unless this contradicts the client's expressed wishes.
Under the principle that a right must have a remedy, people whose rights are violated must be able to go to court, and a legal gap that blocks this violates Article 16.
Article 245(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives the lawyer the right to be present and speak, which reflects these constitutional protections.
The proviso lets prosecutors limit or bar these rights, but current law offers no route to challenge that in court, so the right to sue is clearly harmed.
The challenge to the Ministry of Justice's guideline was not accepted, because the final court ruling did not rely on it and a newer version has replaced it.

who: Lawmakers who must amend the law

raw.answer: A fire department member (listed as a police-rank officer) was dismissed after his rewards and penalties, once offset against each other within one assessment year, added up to two major demerits. He argued the rule treats police and firefighters unfairly compared with ordinary civil servants and that dismissal should be decided by the courts. Taiwan's Constitutional Court held the rule does not violate the Constitution and declined to hear the rest of his petition.
raw.held: The rule requiring dismissal of police personnel whose offset rewards and penalties reach two major demerits in the same assessment year does not conflict with Constitution Articles 7, 18 or 77. The remaining parts of the petition were not accepted.

points.text: The rule applies to firefighters who hold police-officer rank, including the petitioner.
The rule does treat police differently from ordinary civil servants, who are not automatically dismissed at two major demerits but only if the year-end assessment still shows that result.
The purpose is an important public interest: promptly removing police who have broken discipline to the dismissal threshold, to protect people's lives, bodies, freedom, property and public order.
Immediate dismissal is substantially related to that purpose, because police act directly in public life with coercive powers and are held to higher discipline than ordinary civil servants.

The rule does not violate the right to hold public office. It counts rewards and penalties formally decided in the same year, not those whose underlying events happened that year, and authorities are bound by good faith and protection of legitimate expectations.

Having administrative agencies dismiss staff fits the separation of powers, since personnel power is core to administration. Article 77 does not cover administrative discipline, and civil servants can now take dismissals to administrative court.

raw.answer: A Taiwanese citizen married a Vietnamese national, whose application for a spouse-based residence visa was rejected. The citizen sued to have the rejection set aside and to force the government to issue the visa, and the lower court dismissed the suit. The Constitutional Court held that a 2014 Supreme Administrative Court resolution, which says the citizen spouse cannot bring a suit demanding the visa, is not unconstitutional as far as it goes, because it does not rule out the citizen spouse bringing an ordinary suit to cancel the rejection.
raw.held: The resolution only decides that a citizen spouse cannot bring a suit compelling the government to act (a 課予義務訴訟). It does not bar the citizen spouse from exceptionally suing to revoke the rejection under Article 4 of the Administrative Litigation Act, so within that scope it does not violate the constitutional protection of marital freedom (Article 22) or the right to sue (Article 16).

points.text: The court accepted the case even though the petitioner tried to withdraw it, because it is not a unique case and has important constitutional significance.
The right to sue means anyone whose rights or legal interests are harmed can go to court for timely and effective relief.

Marital freedom includes the right to build and run a marriage together with one's spouse. Refusing a foreign spouse's visa limits this for the citizen spouse, who should therefore have a suitable route to administrative remedy.

Only foreign passport holders may apply for a visa under the visa regulations, so the citizen spouse has no legal right to apply for the foreign spouse's visa and cannot bring a suit forcing the government to issue it.

Still, rejecting the foreign spouse's visa is a harmful measure against the citizen spouse's own constitutional rights, so the citizen spouse may exceptionally file an administrative appeal and a suit to revoke it.
The resolution only addresses whether the conditions for a compelling suit are met and does not exclude a revocation suit, so it is not found unconstitutional in that scope.

who: Foreign spouses applying for residence visas

raw.answer: A Taipei court asked whether Article 2 of the Indigenous Status Act is unconstitutional because it recognizes only mountain and plains indigenous peoples, and people who missed the registration window got no status. The Constitutional Court held that the constitution's protection of indigenous peoples covers all Taiwanese Austronesian peoples whose culture and identity still exist, including those beyond the two recognized groups. It found the law unconstitutional to the extent it leaves them out and ordered lawmakers to fix this within 3 years.
raw.held: The protected indigenous peoples include all Austronesian peoples existing in Taiwan that meet the stated conditions, and Article 2 violates the constitution to the extent it leaves them unprotected. Within 3 years of the ruling, the authorities must amend the law or enact a special law, and until then eligible people can apply to the central indigenous affairs authority to have their people recognized.

points.text: The constitution and its amendments do not define indigenous peoples or limit them to mountain and plains indigenous peoples, and do not expressly exclude other indigenous peoples.

Failed amendment proposals to include the Pingpu peoples do not show an intent to exclude them. The amendment provisions on political participation and on cultural protection have different subjects and purposes, so their scopes need not match, and exclusion from protection should be read very narrowly.
Historically, besides the Japanese-era 'highland' peoples, Taiwan has other Austronesian peoples, including the Pingpu, who lived in Taiwan long before Han Chinese became the majority.
Japanese-era household registers marked '熟' or '平' are an objective, consistent historical record that can be used to identify descendants of these peoples.

The protection aims to preserve cultures that still exist, so a people must still keep its language, customs and traditions, and its members must still hold the group identity. Identity is protected by Article 22 and by the amendment provisions, and this includes collective identity.

Because Article 2 covers only mountain and plains indigenous peoples, it leaves other qualifying peoples without legal protection of their status. This conflicts with the identity right and the cultural protection provisions.

who: Siraya and other Pingpu Austronesian peoples and their members
Legislators and the central indigenous affairs authority
People whose or whose ancestors' Japanese-era household registers say '熟' or '平'

raw.answer: A person who lived abroad long-term and had suspended their national health insurance was ordered to pay back premiums for short trips home, and challenged two rules in the insurance law's implementing regulations. The court held that the rules on suspending and resuming coverage break the legal-reservation principle because no law clearly authorized them, so they lose effect within 2 years. It also held that the conditions they set do not violate the proportionality principle, the rights to manage one's own health risks or property, or equality.
raw.held: The two rules (Enforcement Rules Art. 37(1)(2) and Art. 39(1)(2)) violate the legal-reservation principle because no law clearly authorizes them, and they lose effect no later than 2 years after the judgment is announced. Their suspension and resumption conditions, however, are not unconstitutional on proportionality, self-determination over health risks, property or equality grounds.

points.text: Compulsory national health insurance limits people's self-determination over managing their own health risks and affects their property through premiums. Rules on suspending and resuming coverage for people living abroad long-term touch these rights and matter to the system's fairness and finances, so they need a law or a clearly authorizing regulation.
The rules are not mere technical details, so they require a statute or a specific, clear authorization.

The only basis cited was a general clause saying the enforcement rules are set by the competent authority. The health insurance law says nothing about suspending or resuming coverage, so the authority created a system the law does not contain.

On the other rights, the court gives social policy and the state's constitutional duty to run national health insurance more deference. A restriction or unequal treatment is acceptable if its purpose is legitimate and the means are reasonably related to it.

Mandatory resumption on return and a 3-month wait before suspending again serve a legitimate purpose: health care during short visits, avoiding unbalanced premium obligations, and preventing moral hazard. Resumption only restores the prior status, and 3 months of premiums is a limited burden, so the means are reasonably related.

Giving government personnel posted abroad an exception, but not ordinary people, is tied to their need to return briefly on official business on dates they cannot choose. That is a legitimate purpose with a reasonable link, so it does not violate equality.

The court set a 2-year expiry instead of 1 year because fixing a legal-reservation defect requires amending a law, not just a regulation. The legislature keeps room to decide whether to keep a suspension and resumption system, within constitutional limits.

who: People insured under national health insurance who live abroad long-term
People who return home only briefly
Government personnel posted abroad and their families
The health insurance authority and legislature

raw.answer: A company challenged a Ministry of Finance letter (the 1977 letter) that required investment income exempt from tax in a loss year to be netted against that year's loss before the loss could be carried forward to offset later profits. The Constitutional Court held the letter does not violate the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law, and does not raise an equal-treatment problem. It added that it would be better for the rules on how losses are determined to be set by statute or a clearly authorized order.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance letter of 9 March 1977 does not conflict with Article 19 (taxation by law) and raises no problem under Article 7 (equality). The court nevertheless said it is advisable for the standard for determining each period's loss to be set by law or by an order clearly authorized by law.

points.text: The letter only explains how tax offices should determine the 'losses of the previous 10 years' under the loss carry-forward rule. Such an explanation is consistent with taxation by law if it stays within a possible reading of the statute and fits its purpose.
Netting past exempt investment income against past losses does not put that income into the current year's taxable income, so it does not clash with the rule that such income is not taxed.

The rule exempting investment income was not meant to prevent double taxation of the same taxpayer on the same item. The letter counts only the company's real operating loss, which fits the carry-forward rule's aim of measuring ability to pay.

Under the two-tax integration system, exempt investment income was meant to reach individual shareholders through dividends. A loss-making company must cover losses before paying dividends, so this function is weakened in loss years, and the letter does not contradict the system's purpose.
The earlier letters on securities gains and land gains deal with different matters with different purposes, so treating them differently under the letter does not breach equality.

Because the loss carry-forward policy affects public finance, the economy, industry and people's tax burden, the court said the standard for determining losses is better set by statute or a clearly authorized order.

raw.answer: A court referred a drug case to Taiwan's Constitutional Court, asking whether Article 205-2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which lets police take a urine sample from a lawfully arrested suspect against their will, is constitutional. The court held that the rule covers only non-invasive urine collection, where the person urinates on their own. It found the rule lacks the fair-procedure safeguards the Constitution requires, so it will lose effect within 2 years, and interim rules apply until it is amended.
raw.held: Article 205-2 is unconstitutional as it stands and loses effect no later than 2 years after the judgment is announced. Until it is amended, police must ask a prosecutor for a permit before taking urine, or in urgent cases report to the prosecutor within 24 hours. Prosecutors must revoke within 3 days any collection they find should not be allowed, and the person tested may ask a court to revoke it within 10 days. Cases already concluded or still pending under the old rule are handled under current rules.

points.text: The Constitution protects information privacy and freedom from bodily and mental harm. The state may collect personal information by limiting these rights only if it meets Article 23 and follows fair legal procedure, including a chance for remedy.

The rule covers only non-invasive collection, where the person urinates on their own. Invasive methods such as catheterization are not covered, because they would seriously harm the person's rights and police should not be authorized to use them.

Even non-invasive collection against a person's will limits their information privacy and bodily rights, though less severely than invasive collection. It therefore needs proper legal procedure like other compulsory evidence-gathering such as searches and body examinations.

Because the harm is lighter, letting prosecutors decide on non-invasive collection is acceptable. Police may be given exceptional power to act without prior permission, but only with later oversight and a remedy.
Urine evidence can be lost with time, so in urgent cases where delay would prevent preserving evidence, police may collect first and report to a prosecutor afterward.
The rule makes no distinction for urgency, requires no permission, has no prosecutor review afterward, and gives the person no way to seek a remedy. That does not meet fair legal procedure.

raw.answer: Two petitioners, a judge hearing a lawsuit and a person in a compensation case, asked whether a rule requiring land once provided for farmland irrigation use to keep being used that way, with no compensation, violates the constitutional protection of property. The court held that the rule can stand only if privately owned land used this way is backed by a legal basis such as a lease or purchase, or else is expropriated with fair compensation. The government must draw up compensation plans within 3 years.
raw.held: Where privately owned land must keep being used for irrigation and the government has not obtained a right to use it by lease, purchase or other means, the owner has borne a special sacrifice. The land must then be expropriated with fair compensation, and plans and funding must be set up within 3 years so this is completed gradually within a reasonable time.

points.text: Property rights protect an owner's freedom to use, profit from and dispose of their property. If the state turns private property into public-use property without a legal basis, the owner bears a special sacrifice and must be compensated through expropriation.

Irrigation land is public-use property serving an especially important public interest, such as farming, the economy and people's livelihoods. It has been used continuously for a long time, so it should stay in use unless it is no longer needed and is formally retired.

Owners of such land must tolerate its use for irrigation and cannot freely use it, so their property rights are seriously restricted. The state therefore needs a legal basis, such as a lease or purchase. Without one, it must expropriate with compensation and set up plans within 3 years.

Official figures show that acquiring rights to the land has been slow and the dedicated fund is far too small. Authorities should set a deadline, raise funds, and consider ways other than full expropriation to obtain rights.

Privately owned land used this way may serve only irrigation purposes and must be used in the least harmful way. Authorities should review each case and formally retire land no longer needed for irrigation.

who: Private owners of land used for irrigation
The government agency in charge of irrigation land

raw.answer: National Taiwan University did not want to renew an assistant professor's contract, but the teacher's complaint bodies reversed that, and the Ministry of Education's central review committee rejected the university's further complaint. The university sued, but the courts refused to hear it, relying on a Supreme Administrative Court meeting resolution that said universities cannot sue over such decisions. The Constitutional Court held that this part of the resolution violates the Constitution, so a public university may go to court over such a decision.
raw.held: The part of the Supreme Administrative Court's June 2017 resolution saying a public university cannot take administrative court action against a re-complaint decision that does not uphold its non-renewal of a teacher is unconstitutional. It conflicts with academic freedom (Art. 11) and the right to sue (Art. 16), and it stops being applied from the day the judgment is announced.

points.text: The right to sue means anyone whose rights are harmed must be able to seek court relief, and a university whose self-governance is harmed by the education authority's supervision should be able to sue too.
Not renewing a teacher is a university's contract-based act as a contracting party, not an exercise of delegated public power, even though it greatly affects the teacher.

The teacher laws set up complaint and re-complaint procedures but do not expressly bar a university from suing when supervision harms its self-governance. Reading the resolution as excluding universities would leave those laws open to constitutional doubt.

The re-complaint is a special dispute mechanism used when internal handling fails, and the central committee decides it in the name of the central authority as an administrative act. A public university is a rights-holder in academic freedom with self-governance, so it may sue if that decision harms it.
So the resolution's reasoning that the university is merely the party whose measure is under review, and so cannot sue, does not hold up.

who: Education authorities (Ministry of Education and its review committee)

raw.answer: Four people who had lost civil defamation-type cases challenged a Civil Code provision that lets courts order a wrongdoer to take 'appropriate measures' to restore a victim's reputation. In practice courts used it to order forced public apologies. The Constitutional Court held that the provision cannot be read to include court-ordered apologies, because that would violate free speech and, for individuals, freedom of thought.
raw.held: The 'appropriate measures' in Civil Code Article 195(1), second part, cannot include a court judgment ordering the wrongdoer to apologize, and the earlier Interpretation No. 656 is changed to that extent. The four petitioners may file for retrial within 30 days of receiving the judgment, and where an apology was already carried out, the retrial court may replace it with another measure at the victim's request, without undoing the apology or allowing that new measure to be enforced.

points.text: Forcing someone to apologize interferes with free speech, including the freedom not to speak. It forbids silence and compels a self-negating statement, so it faces strict review.
Restoring a victim's reputation is a legitimate aim, but it is doubtful that every such case involves a especially important public interest, since some disputes are purely private.

Less harmful alternatives exist, such as publishing a notice of the victory or the judgment in the media, and a court can also encourage an apology. A forced apology is therefore not the least harmful necessary means, and it is also doubtful that an insincere apology truly helps the victim.

When the wrongdoer is an individual, a forced apology also violates freedom of thought, which is absolutely protected. It turns a legal judgment into the person's own moral judgment, causing self-denial and harming conscience and dignity.
A legal person (such as a company) cannot claim freedom of thought, so for them only the free speech problem applies.

Where an apology was already carried out, the retrial court should not apply Civil Procedure Code Article 505-1 or order restoration of the prior state, to avoid a second injury to the victim. The replacement measure cannot be enforced, so the dispute can end sooner.

who: Defendants ordered by courts to apologize

raw.answer: A person challenged Taiwan's National Health Insurance Administration for passing health insurance data, including personal data, to research databases for uses beyond running health insurance. The court found the personal data law's rule allowing de-identified data to be used for medical or health statistics and research constitutional. It also found that the surrounding legal framework falls short in several ways and ordered lawmakers to fix them within 3 years.
raw.held: Article 6(1)(4) of the Personal Data Protection Act is held consistent with the clarity and proportionality principles and does not violate the constitutional privacy right. However, the lack of an independent oversight body, of clear statutory rules on the health insurance database, and of any right to request a stop to secondary use are unconstitutional or likely so, and must be fixed within 3 years; if no law is made in time, people may ask to stop the secondary use.

points.text: The rule's wording is understandable enough: 'cannot identify a specific person' means directly identifying information is removed, though indirect identification may remain possible, so the clarity principle is met.

Personal health insurance data stays identifiable in principle, and the rule lets agencies use it without consent, so it limits the constitutional information privacy right and must meet strict review.
The rule's purpose, advancing medicine and public health through statistics and research, is a particularly important public interest.
The means is the least harmful and proportionate: it limits users, purposes and necessity and requires de-identification, while fully anonymous data would lose research value.
Taiwan's laws as a whole lack an independent body overseeing personal data protection, which leaves privacy protection insufficient.

Key matters of how the insurance agency stores, processes and shares health data with others lack clear rules at statute level, only agency-made rules, which breaches the statutory reservation principle.

People have a constitutional right to ask for use of their data to stop, but the laws give no such right for secondary use of health insurance data, and the existing Article 11 does not cover this situation.

who: People covered by national health insurance
National Health Insurance Administration and Ministry of Health and Welfare
Academic research institutions and public agencies
Legislators and the authorities who must revise the laws

raw.answer: The case was brought by people whose mothers were indigenous and fathers were not, and who were refused indigenous status because they did not take the indigenous parent's surname or a traditional indigenous name. The Constitutional Court held that this requirement violates the constitutional protection of indigenous identity and equality, and told the authorities to fix the law within two years.
raw.held: The rule that a child of an indigenous and a non-indigenous parent gets indigenous status only by taking the indigenous parent's surname or a traditional name is unconstitutional, as are the related provisions that apply it. Lawmakers have 2 years to amend; if they do not, the rule expires and such children get indigenous status and may register it. The petitioners' other requests were not accepted for review.

points.text: The right to indigenous identity is a highly protected personal right under the Constitution, so the rule had to pass strict review.
Promoting cultural identity is a particularly important public interest, but distributing state benefits is not enough by itself to justify limiting this right.
Requiring the indigenous parent's surname is doubtful as a way to promote identity, because indigenous peoples traditionally had no surnames and such surnames are Han Chinese names.

Names are only a formal sign of identity, and registering the child as indigenous already shows identity; requiring a name before status is not the least harmful means, and gentler options exist, such as adding a traditional name alongside the existing name.

The rule treats children of two indigenous parents differently from children of one indigenous parent, which is a classification by race or ethnic group needing strict review, and it fails that review.
The difference makes little sense: children with a higher share of indigenous ancestry must show more identity than those with a lower share, which the court called baseless and arbitrary.

who: Children of one indigenous and one non-indigenous parent
Indigenous mothers who married non-indigenous men
The petitioners, who were denied indigenous status
Lawmakers and the indigenous affairs authorities
